he does not know whether the metal is fine or coarse. On a scale without markings, how can one determine its weight?"
Jutang Chacha was asked by a monk, "The student has not yet understood the timing; I beg the Master for instruction.
Chacha said, "The pines and bamboos are uneven, thin mist gathers upon them; the peaks and ridges are layered, the moon rises late over them.

As the monk prepared to offer a reply, Chacha said, "Before the armor is even donned, the thief’s body is already exposed. The monk asked, "Why is that? Chacha said, "The refined bamboo before the frost is not cut; the water..."
The followers of Mozi boast of dragons upon the sea; the monk circles the meditation seat once, laughs loudly, and departs. Chacha said:
"To eat a snail with eyes closed—what a bitter and sour experience!"
The Master said: "Since Tong'an already knows the thief’s identity has been revealed, why does he still harbor the thief?
Not knowing to close one's eyes while eating a snail is also like drawing one's bow after the thief has fled."
To cite Zen Master Deshan Xuanjian: A monk approached him and assumed a wrestling stance.
Deshan said, "Such rudeness deserves a blow from my hand. The monk brushed his sleeves and departed.
Deshan said, "Even granting you this much, you have only attained half. The monk turned around and shouted. Deshan struck him, saying, "It must be I who strikes you before it is right. The monk...
The monk said, "There are people with clear eyes in all directions. Yunmen said, "Naturally there are eyes.
The monk opened his eyes wide, and the cat went out. Yunmen said, "The Yellow River clears once every three thousand years."

The Master said: "I have been carrying the staff along all this time. Where would you look for Deshan? Although this monk’s merit from his military service is high, he does not realize that he has been pinned down by Deshan right here."
One day Jingu held up a pillow and said, "Everyone calls this a pillow;
Jingu says it is not. A monk asked, "I do not know what you, the Master, call it? Jingu held up the pillow again.
The monk said, "If that is so, then I shall follow it accordingly. Jingu asked, "What do you call it? The monk said, "A pillow. Jingu said: [The text ends here.]
[The monk] fell into the hollow of Jinfeng.
The Master said, "Do you wish to recognize Jinfeng? A deep pool does not permit the azure dragon to lie.
He then cited the case of Yantou when Sansheng came to visit him. Yantou said, "There is no need to spread out your napkin; here there is no leftover broth."
Fàn asked, "If there were such a thing, where would you place it? Xuánshèu immediately struck him. Xuánshèu caught the staff and pushed it onto the bed.
Xuánshèu clapped his hands once. Xuánshèu then covered Xuánshèu with his sitting mat (zuoju), whereupon Xuánshèu cried out to the blue heavens and departed.
The Master said: "Their power is equal and their strength is even; each has a way to turn and a path to life.
As for these two great elders, they are truly nothing more than leftover gruel and rice. Why, then, is it so disarrayed? Where the clash of arms arises, it is difficult to roll up the banners."

A Dharma Talk for Shui (the junior disciple of Yanxi) Master Shui, a junior disciple of Yanxi, came from Shuangjing to Bashi during the summer to seek a Dharma talk. I immediately spoke to him, saying: "Huangbo’s three blows of the staff."
The Chan of Guizong’s single flavor is the most supreme method for raising a child.

At its highest level, a single word or half-phrase is like a bolt of raw iron, leaving no room for chewing or gnawing. Even at the next level down, how could it be compared to using flowery words and sweet talk, or bribing with gold and fine food?
Your teacher occupies Beishan as the patriarch of this age; he is a gate of raw iron.
Limit yourself. Wrap the scale-beam in cotton; do not peep or spy from too close a distance. To abandon one’s kin for those who are distant is the disciple turning his back on the teacher;
it is not the fault of the teacher. When a son returns before his father, there is no way to bypass the intimacy of the father-son bond;
yet the transmission of the Buddha-dharma is not a private matter. It is like a lion teaching its cub at the edge of the Red Cliff, or a magnificent eagle nesting in a tree.

At the end, he threw himself back and soared forth, like a broken mirror emerging from its nest; when one does not see the teacher at the critical moment, only then can one truly claim the lineage of one’s father.
The two masters, Shishi and Xuanzhao, went to Mount Taibai with resolute intent;
they must have possessed the eyes of certainty. Possessing the eyes of certainty, they were surely able to discern the great matter of certainty.
At other times, he pointed to the monasteries of Siming as a sea toward which monks from all quarters would rush, every spring following winter.
At the very beginning, one must certainly set aside thirty or forty units [of space] to await those who come from afar.
The staff is not moved lightly, nor are the feet placed down lightly; this is why one sells one’s cotton robe and travels far to Mount Yi, giving rise to the "turning-new" smile.
Under the words of the One-Eyed Dragon, how could one reach such a state without possessing a resolute will? To possess a resolute will is to possess the eye of resolution.
This is not merely a matter of passing through a narrow pass. The Taibai Peak rises twenty *li* high; its pines do not diminish their ancient power as they reach toward the heavens.
Although it is said that the gates of the pavilions open without the need to snap one's fingers, one must further know that once entered, there is a gate that closes behind one.
Although one may penetrate silver mountains and iron walls, this barrier cannot be penetrated. How can one penetrate this barrier?
It requires resolute courage; it does not depend on Baoshan’s further verbal elaborations.

Master Qi of Xichan was shown that in the past, when Shushan heard the words of Lan’an regarding "having a phrase" and "having no phrase," he immediately sold his cotton robe and, undaunted by hardship, went straight to the Western Monastery.
He sought to parry Lan’an’s sharp verbal thrusts, yet he could not withstand Lan’an’s single smile. This was Shushan.
There was simply nothing more that could be done. With a distant, long journey ahead and a state of mind filled with indignation, how could one’s heart be set on seeking the Way at such a time?
Lǎn’ān’s silence was not due to a lack of secrecy; rather, it was out of pity for those who could not pass through the gate of a single laugh.

It was the One-Eyed Dragon who pointed it out for him and broke through his delusions; at that moment, he came to possess such majestic authority. Could there not have been others like him? Why then point specifically to the One-Eyed Dragon?

It is because he possessed the eyes of the higher realm and recognized the functional pivot of the higher realm. He was like one who has already drawn a crossbow bolt weighing ten thousand *jin*—it is simply a matter of releasing it.
Thus, the spiritual blade and precious sword are constantly manifest before him, appearing with a clarity that pierces through all. How could this be otherwise?
Is there any difference? Only when one is summoned by the light and pierced through by the opportune point can one finally realize that there is a blade within Lazy An’s smile.

The man of Qi studied at West Temple, traveling back and forth between east and west; this was surely because he had heard something and sought it out, or perhaps because he admired the great furnace and sought refinement therein.
Yet, by abandoning what is near to seek what is distant, they run counter to one another. At the place where the stone ox sleeps, the lychees have ripened.

At that time, his thirst for inquiry was so great that he swallowed it upon hearing it enter his mouth; with a throat-clearing laugh, he finally believed in Lǎn'ān, yet realized that [Lǎn'ān] had never truly been absent.
The One-Eyed Dragon was not present at Míngzhāo.
The Patriarch showed that when the Honored One Bodhidharma came from the West, he sat facing a wall for nine years before the Second Patriarch finally approached him;

there were no other words exchanged, save that [Bodhidharma] spoke only of how one must undergo long-term hardship and toil to achieve realization—that which is like true ghee or a poisonous drug. Only by standing in the snow and severing his own arm did [Huike] attain peace.
Furthermore, how could one endure toil and suffering for long before reaching a state of courageous exertion?
In a single *kṣaṇa*, one may enter the Great Ocean of the Tathāgata’s Nirvāṇa—just as Linji did under Huangbo’s staff, or Baizhang under Mazu’s shout.
It was not Linji who could not receive Huangbo’s staff, nor was it Baizhang who could not withstand Mazu.
Only by raising this shout can one truly revitalize the ancestral founder’s school.
Wandering through prefectures and counties, whenever he encountered those whose eyes were fixed and whose movements were steady, he acted with the urgency of a lion attacking its prey.

His vision of Master Ding was such that he wished to crush this "bed-wetting ghost" to death, thereby enabling Xuefeng and Yantou to clench their fists so they penetrate their palms. He was able to select a master of the fundamental lineage.
In this fundamental monastic community, one forgets the passage of years and seasons through diligent toil, establishing resolute faith.
Thus, not only does the master not fail the student, but the student also does not betray their own eye of discernment. If faith is not resolute, even the straw sandals and staff can deceive one.
When the Patriarch came from Jingwu to Bashi to seek words of Dharma, he was appropriately addressed by the former patriarch as follows:
With the Master as your model, you may perhaps reach far; thus, name and reality will correspond. Yet for Poshan to speak in this way is like drawing legs on a snake.
Within the gate of the patch-robed monks, there is neither Buddha nor Patriarch. O Patriarchs and those above them, stay alert!
Verse:
Celestial robes arise from conditions;
the furnace for smelting gold grows cold as the seasons change. Having once traveled along this path, the tide rises upon the sands, bringing the chill.
The wild geese have flown away; the creeping vines and sprouts grow once more.

Paying homage at Mingzhao’s stupa, one finds the wind already harsh and headstrong; returning further to a warm place, one sinks into self-concealment, only to leave behind a trail that endures for a thousand ages.
Traces! You have come in vain to eat the white rice of Luoshan.
At Shuian, your karmic conditions for this one night’s stay were clear and not easily cast aside; with his old fist, he sought a mortal enemy. One should not let one's natural endowment go to waste.
From that time on, no one dared to emerge.

Paying homage to the Mingjiao Pagoda, he acted according to his words, as brilliant as the sun and stars. A solitary pillar to stem the tide, it stands tall and firm. How could one carve [this inscription] upon the cliffs by the lake?
Stone. Engraved upon it is only a memorial for the Venerable Monk Zuanseng.
At the Su Xi Mu Hu Sitting Meditation Rock, the opportune moment suddenly manifests:
the duck swallows the snail. What can be done about these sheer cliffs and precipitous walls? All are but the squatting and sitting at Su Xi.
It is not merely that the shadows of the green cypresses sway;

within the wind-blown banners and shadows of the Arhat Stupa, the eyes are dazed and confused. Though you claim to be a connoisseur, you do not yet know; after all, has the thorn in your breast been removed?
Attained. Cold pines for a thousand ages replace sorrow and grief.

The traces of the Buddha appear and vanish amidst sparks and lightning; even when cliffs crumble and rocks split, it remains difficult to repay his kindness. If you let go for a single step, do you still know?
No. The Buddha was an old bhikṣu from the Western Heaven.

The footprints upon the stone where his cloth bag left its mark shall flow for ten thousand ages like the Great River; how could one have gathered up the mess at that time? It was simply because his heels were not touched down.
The earth; moreover, a stone by the Wà Bridge remains.
At Tàoguān Hermitage, the ancient trees still stand with their trunks hollowed out. Moss upon the gray cliffs is the seal of former times. Clouds follow the ten carriages back to Yí.
Luò. The moon shines year after year upon the peaks above the lake.
The numinous elder returned to Shǔ;

half his life spent in pure austerity, his patched robe was free from worldly distinctions. Only the snow accumulated on the *shā* courtyard knew him. His eyes bore the colors of the East and South Seas.
Bi: Do not look at Mount Emei through mist and rain.
This humble old man dwells in the Jingshan Hermitage amidst a heap of dung-fire, unable to conceal himself;
the taro roots pierce straight through the nine layers of fragrance. Deeply locked by clouds and mist is Mount Jingshan.
In the mountain hamlet, the sound of the bell from the monastery sends off the setting sun.

At Mount Ao, one is received with hospitality until one attains peaceful sleep amidst a full meal. The roads to the east, west, south, and north all lead through; at the stroke of midnight, the ghosts marry.
Calamity! None surpass Yantou and Xuefeng.

Inspecting Qiaoyuan (Qiao Lingxian met Songyuan) throughout the Jiatai and Kāixī eras—who else remains in the monastic courts of the Chan school? Tall bamboos and ancient pines stand solemnly in the cold.
Form. It is just like when asking the way to Cold Spring:

at Huishan, one brews tea with a broken earthen jar, drawing clear, cold water at dawn; the stone cauldron is moved from ruined steps to boil it, as the pine winds from ten thousand ravines serve a single guest.
Sipping [tea], I walk by the water with both sleeves tucked into my robe.
Having found this monkey at Lingyin, my heart finds no rest;
it is most poignant. How much more so when the sound of the monkeys enters the night so frequently? From this moment on, beneath Feilai Peak...
At the temple, how many more heart-rending people are added?
Venerable Jian returns to Shu;
the moon over Mount Emei stirs ancient sentiments. Its reflection flows into the Yu River, twice as clear. Dust is cleared away and light arises across the lakes and seas.
Guest: Returning home, you once again vie with the moon for brilliance.

As for meeting Master Foku—who has long been known by reputation—there is no need for further discussion. You have traveled in vain as far as the village outside Fangfeng County; more than half of spring’s radiance is now shrouded in mist and rain.
Inside. Clearly, the gate of Baishan has been shut.

A verse for the Venerable Shou seeking the "eye" throughout the various quarters: If one's ability is at variance with the Way, do not recklessly spread out the cooking cloth. One must know that a single peak encompasses the world.
Xiu: Originally he flew here from the Western Kingdom of India.
He has sent the Venerable Sui to come from Mount Heng to look at this painting. His two eyes do nothing but gaze upward; let him lower his head once and we shall meet.
Departing, one finally knows that the Jade Desk is loftiest and coldest.
When Chan Master Fu took charge of a monastery, he ascended to Xuedou;

his ancient spirit was like a rainbow long coiled in submission. Grasping the thatched roof, he entered the deep mountains with ease, yet even before Changgeng spoke, his inner resolve was already known.
Severed. Cold debts must now be repaid.
I send this to the venerable Qi of Jiaoshan to see Guangyuan Yun-tuan;
Guangyuan has exhausted his city of sorrow. It is not necessarily that his heart and liver were forged from iron. When speaking of it, one thinks of the foot of Mount Shigong.
The matter is settled, like a monkey’s third cry;

beyond the forty-nine turns of the flying birds that escort [him] to Mount Qing of Yandang, his patched robe still bears the chill of the mountain clouds. The misty waves of lake and sea are cast wide open.
The eye: withered trees and stones lie within the Yan Mountains.

Master Gong seeks [this state where] the western wind blows rain across the skies of Wu; not touching pole or line upon a single fishing boat, he remains in solitude, yet would still greedily crave fragrant bait.
The flavor: upon the rivers and lakes, how many smoke-filled straw raincoats drift?
Master Liaoweng’s public case is but a forced mold; failing to understand its deep concealment, he brings trouble upon himself. "If it is I who has killed, then I shall pay the debt."
Life! How can one’s heart be so solitary in old age?
An ancient mirror does not know how many kalpas it has been obscured by dust; its original form and pattern cannot be distinguished clearly. A single piece of bronze has been worn away.
Exhausted. Only when there is no longer any place for polishing does the light first arise.

The six windows of the dream-house are deeply closed within the great magnolia palace; with a single pillow and pure breeze, in the blink of an eye, from the end of kalpas until now, the Buddha and...
The Patriarch: "At the top of the tower, one knows how many times the bell has struck. Huan’an:
"The void splits open and the ocean dries up; man dwells within the shadows of foam-bubbles. Eyes closed at dusk, eyes open—"
Daylight. Where does the moonlight ascend upon the coral?
The blind old man says there is no dharma outside the mind; though Shoushan has eyes, they lack light. He strikes with a blind staff and brandishes the club.
Go! Throughout the earth and under heaven, calamities and misfortunes arise.
The ancient vessel’s single sail does not open without cause; it pierces through the towering waves and white surges. In the blink of an eyebrow, ten million [obstacles are overcome].
Kalpa. Who was it that washed his feet and boarded the boat?
King Shouxiu is eighty years old;

his Way is honored and his virtue is as lofty as a jade pillar. He further consolidates the support of the state and upholds the weighty statutes and laws. At eighty, he supports himself with a *lingshou* staff.
With staff in hand, all gaze upon the Elder Star of the Southern Pole.
In his hidden chamber, Mañjuśrī appears in person; his traces are entirely unimpeded, yet he obstructs the ten directions with a single fathom.
Understood. How can one strike [the lute] to manifest the entire body and praise the Buddhas and Patriarchs as they emerge from the mountains?
At midnight he leaped over the city walls; at the hour of the middle watch he saw the stars, yet beneath the clear blue sky and bright sun, the Great Way was not traversed.
The mud and water beneath his feet grew ever deeper; in the end, when did he ever attain the Way and achieve realization?

The Avalokiteśvara who practices the Way hears all things yet does not dwell upon them. When karmic consciousness is in a state of frantic bustle, even the emptiness that makes emptiness vanish is extinguished; it is difficult to conceal oneself throughout the entire world.
Suddenly setting out on foot, toward which direction will you go?
In the Lion Kingdom, the Lion-Aspect Avalokiteśvara saves sentient beings according to their kind; amidst the rocky crags and ocean tides, he roars without ceasing.
Those who wish to see the true lion cub should contemplate his voice herein.
The Fish Basket Guanyin vainly combs her spring wind-tossed hair, which hangs down over both temples; the nightingale cries out across the branches of falling blossoms.
Every house has its guests from Dragon Gate—whom shall she bring these fine carp to sell?

Avalokiteśvara’s perfect clarity pervades the ten directions; his manifestations are manifold. When the pure pitcher is held in the eyes, when he sits upon the Paṇḍaka stone, and when the willow branch enters his hand—every drop is indeed a single drop.

Trample upon the lotus petals throughout the countless oceans of Buddha-lands; manifesting bodies everywhere, like the sun at its zenith atop each lotus leaf—one should practice contemplation in this manner.
This is the twenty-fifth of the Perfect Penetrations.
Baguishi (Pu-tai Heshang) [III]:
Dragging his cloth bag and grasping his black staff, he wanders through the streets and marketplaces; this is no idle strolling.
Relying on his cloth bag to dream, what clarity of mind could there be? If he encounters one of the true practitioners of the Way, they will call him awake and tell him to go drink tea.
Carrying this on one shoulder is no light matter; what kind of tattered rag is this? Though you look behind and ahead, you do not realize you have lost the pavilion.
Bodhidharma crossed the reeds. (2)

The waters of the Yangtze River are boundless; even the reeds and rushes can be broken. Having departed from the Liang court, yet not yet reached the gates of Wei—this regret, amidst the waves, to whom shall I speak?
Shattering the six heterodox schools, he opened the five petals of the flower. In the Western Heaven and this land, there was no cinnabar.
Fenggan comes and goes across the place where the fierce beast roams; he moves together with Hanzhu and Shishi. Without investigation, they expose one another like thieves in a fire;
to claim that he is Amitābha—what evidence is there for this?
Hanshan chants five characters while enduring hunger; for ten years he has forgotten the path home. Whether he clothes himself or not, he laughs heartily—a single outburst that cannot be contained.
Such a phrase is the true Mañjuśrī, the non-dual Mañjuśrī. *Sulu-sili, sili-sulu*.
Picked up, it has no place of origin; set down, it leaves traces. One laughs, yet does not understand what the meaning is. How much mess can one ever sweep away?
The ocean of suffering is boundless; the practice of vows is boundless. To call this Samantabhadra is not to call him Samantabhadra.
Hanshan and Shide (putting down their brooms, sitting facing a cliff rock, gazing at the moon):
Having set aside their brooms, they sit together in a mountain cave; their eyes gaze without ceasing and their mouths speak without rest.
They think that even on Mount Emei or Mount Wutai, there is no such bright moon as this.
The Boatman Monk did not merely dangle his light boat in play; with a single stroke before it could unfold, his life was as thin as a thread.
With eyes bright and clear beyond the misty waves, when would the clever *śrāmaṇera* arrive?
Master Yushan picked up a bright pearl and smiled with an open mouth; he said that when the dust is cleared, one merely turns back into dust.
If one lacks the capacity to directly accept this, one will bring shame upon the donkey’s single leap.

Zheng Huangniu has returned from the rivers and seas; how many years have passed? Yet he gazes upon the winds and mists from atop the ox’s back. Ten out of ten, this is a phrase spoken with inverted heels;
the myriad phenomena can never be fully grasped.
The morning sun pierces through the tattered robe;
how much can this ragged garment hold? It cannot be fully mended, nor can its holes be entirely filled. At midnight in Silla, the sun’s orb is red;
when has a thread ever been able to pass through it?
The skeletal frame is cold; the coarse woolen robe is cold. It does not face the morning sun; it is difficult to grasp.
At this very moment, the great earth bursts into flames. Facing the moon, one finishes the remaining sutra.
(2) The moon is in the sky; the characters are on the paper. Regarding this sutra, have you finished it yet? The mouth is like nostrils; the eyes are like eyebrows. Relying upon—

Sitting before the light and shadow, the mind becomes transparently clear and the eyes open wide. The final word is beyond all contrivance; without ever unrolling a scroll, the bright moon comes of its own accord.
Master Wuzu roused himself with an iron-like resolve;
leaping from the cliff, he overturned the spearhead. Lacking hooves yet possessing horns, he attained the keen hearing of the deaf old man and struck with a sudden peal of thunder.
Riding upon the clouds of Yunchao, he scattered great hailstones. At a distance he seemed approachable, yet the closer one drew, the more remote he became. He grasped the dead.

A fire-starter who kindles the blazing flames of the Dragon Palace with gentle and fierce fires, and who, with his broad and long tongue, proclaims the True Holy Truth while receiving the profound grace of the Son of Heaven.
Some may call him the one who, like Miam and Poan, leaps over fences and vaults through windows to uphold the ancestral house;
yet who would know him to be a peerless master of the "cold frost and icy flames" of Xiushui and Huangmei?
Master Dayue carries a single board and has lost his livelihood; seeing that Old Neng has an aperture at the crown of his head, he recognizes that Bimbasara holds no pitchfork in his hand.
A thunderclap resounds, startling many slumbering dragons and snakes; with a hand that moves freely between square and round, there is not a trace of flaw. Returning, he lowers [the board].
With the celestial clouds as wings, he recalled the ancient home of the Jewel Grove (Pāṭaliputra) and swept away the territory where foxes and hares had run wild.

Along the boundaries of the sacred precincts, he adjusted matters of weight and measure, ensuring that the shade of the Bodhi tree would flourish forever and that withered faces would bloom like rosy clouds. Were it not for iron trees blossoming with flowers, how could such a thing be possible?
Dongpo could not be moved by gain or loss from his natural constancy; in Danyang he was as at ease as in the Jade Hall.
He went back and forth borrowing books and even borrowing rain-cloaks, unaware of the rain-soaked steps in the land of miasmic fogs.
The fields of Yuanming have long been overgrown with weeds; "Return, Let Us Go," he sang as he took up his hoe. With a serene gaze, he beheld the sightless;
the chrysanthemums year after year remain beyond description.
Governor Yang has perfected the elixir of immortality prior to the primordial beginning; his Way extends its salvation to the furthest reaches of the earth.

He bears the burden of a distinguished reputation and noble lineage, yet has forgotten the habits of a lifetime spent in wealth and honor. He acts and rests according to the moment, neither rigid nor compulsive, wielding the Mount Sumeru of his resolve.
Even my brush finds it difficult to describe this quality of a refined gem.
The Minor Buddhist Service Supervisor,
Mind-Monitoring Abbot, has entered the stupa.
The mind is exhausted; mountains and peaks sink away. Entering birth and exiting death, one wanders freely and at will. When departing in this manner, what then?
A stone casket beneath a cliff; a name that shall not be worn away for a thousand ages.
The fixed kitchen steward enters the stupa;
fundamentally there is no gate—through what could he enter? Having set down the basket and wooden ladle, he conceals his body until no trace remains.
He casts down his bones and says: "It is because of these spiritual remains."

The Senior Monk Quan held up a torch and said: "There is the provisional and there is the real; there is the guest and there is the host. A truly nimble monk would know where it lands the moment it is lit.
But tell me, what do you take as your basis? Fierce flames reaching to the heavens—red, with no place for you to settle."
As for the "location":

when the Elder Guàn opened the coffin, two five-hundred-cash pieces were found to be originally a single string of one-thousand-cash coins. Without reason, he searched east and west until he arrived at the side of Cold Spring Pavilion.
The furnace blazes fiercely; how can one enter? Upādhyāya Guàn has raised his banners and drums.
Venerable Rùn enters the pagoda:
on the mountain slope there is stone that has endured for a thousand years; at the bottom of the well, the spring never dries for a single day. Here, receive it directly.

Just as he was about to act, he saw the sacred relics standing solemnly before him; the coins were of full weight. Once the sound of the *ghaṇṭā* had ceased, Venerable Run, the *karmadāna*, could no longer turn back from his regret.
Neng, the *vihārasvāmin*, lit the funeral pyre.

A single expanse of empty stillness; celestial flowers fall like rain. Within the flash of lightning, one departs and another arrives, yet for the moment, they do not know where their tea bowl has fallen.
Neng, the guest prefect, assents: "Go drink your tea."
The Elder Guang said:

"The ocean of birth and death is most vast and deep; it is like a ferry crossing where one may encounter drifting and sinking. Before even a single bubble has arisen, when suddenly a fire breaks out—how is it then?
He cast down a torch and said: "It matters whether you open your eyes or close them."

Although the place where Chan Master Nangu Shouzuo held the torch is the same, its application differs. At the profound pivot beyond the ordinary, he shook the high wind; from beginning to end, his single integrity was unalterable.
Amidst the coming and going of birth and death, he moved with ease. To let go is easy—the four seas follow one standard—but to hold fast is difficult.

A central pillar amidst the turbulent current, he was accustomed to enduring the harsh blows of evil fists atop the Jasper Terrace and Mushroom Peak. He shared the seat and upheld the essential principles of the school on the lakes and mountains at Shuangjing.
Pointing out the great tree that provides shade, he opened the eyes of humans and devas.

Although he did not join the ranks of the water-buffalo, he further manifested the fierce majesty of a lion. When the frost withered and the snow grew old, the dream was shattered and the night watch ended. At the very end—
The total presentation: like a flash of lightning or a spark from flint. By the time you blink your eyes, the ancient Buddha has already passed away.

When Master Wuzhu of Yuyang took the first step toward the coffin, there was no prior arrangement. When questioned, his spiritual pivot struck him square in the face; from this point on, karmic debts could no longer be obstructed.
Attained! Before others, he suddenly stirred up wind and thunder. Where Fohui attained it, Fozhao did not know; where Fohui employed it, Tuigou did not understand.
Appearing and disappearing, rolling and unfolding, he practiced long-term samādhi. He dwelt on famous mountains for six years, dwelling without a fixed dwelling.

One of great practice traverses this path by practicing non-practice. Pressed to the limit until the year ends and the age is exhausted, suddenly the bowstring is drawn with the force of a thousand *qun*.
Neither ordinary beings nor sages know his trace; he leaves all the patch-robed monks of the world in doubt. As empty space cracks open, the Master of Yují is fully revealed.
If you wish to see Chan Master Fohui now, it is easy to shift one's body; yet if you wish to see Chan Master Fohui...
To change one's step is difficult. It is neither difficult nor easy. The wondrous trace is not where the monkeys cry. (The Verse on Passing Away says:
"Neither ordinary beings nor sages know its trace; it slips away from the void with a loud crack.")
The Great Man’s marks of National Teacher Shishan entered the Patriarchs’ Hall.
After his *nirvāṇa*, there was water that could not wet them and brushstrokes that could not capture them.

The descendants of Shishan have, from this point on, directly departed from the old molds; they shift positions and turn the pivot, entering the marketplace to extend a helping hand through the "curtain of night-brightness."
The outer grasses are lush and verdant; the moon is bright upon the lapis lazuli pavilion. This alone is the Great Human Mark of the Stone Mountain Master.
Through birth and death, coming and going, he has never shifted. Is he subject to arrangement? Holding up the name tablet, he says: "The title is clear."
